Another
uh-NUTH-ur
adj., pron.
From Old English an (one) and other. Webster 1828: not the same; different; one more, in addition. The English word hides a distinction the Greek New Testament makes plainly — between allos, another of the same kind, and heteros, another of a different kind — and Galatians 1 turns on it.

Biblical Definition

Another looks like the plainest word in the Bible, and it carries one of its sharpest edges. Paul writes to a church drifting toward a rival message: I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel: Which is not another (Galatians 1:6-7). In English that reads like a contradiction. In Greek it is exact. The first another is heteros, a different kind of thing; the second is allos, another of the same kind. Paul is saying: they are peddling a gospel of a different kind, which is not a second gospel at all, because there is only one. A rival gospel is not an alternative; it is a counterfeit. The same distinction blesses in the other direction. Christ promises, I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter (John 14:16) — allos, another of the same kind. The Spirit is not a lesser substitute for the departing Son but a Comforter of the same divine order, which is a plain testimony to His deity. And Paul warns the Corinthians against another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel (2 Corinthians 11:4). The whole doctrine of the exclusivity of Christ sits inside this small word.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ANOTHER as not the same; different: as, we have another task to perform. Also, one more, in addition to a former number; and any other, any different person indefinitely.

expand to see more

ANOTHER, a. [of an or one, and other.] — Not the same; different; as, we have one form of government; France has another. One more, in addition to a former number. Any other; any different person, indefinitely.

Webster’s first two senses are exactly the Greek pair. Not the same; different is heteros. One more, in addition to a former number is allos. English collapses them into one spelling; the New Testament keeps them apart, and Galatians 1:6-7 is unreadable until the reader knows it.

Key Scripture

Galatians 1:6 — "I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel:"

Galatians 1:7 — "Which is not another; but there be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ."

John 14:16 — "And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever;"

2 Corinthians 11:4 — "For if he that cometh preacheth another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or if ye receive another spirit, which ye have not received, or another gospel, which ye have not accepted, ye might well bear with him."

Isaiah 42:8 — "I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images."

Modern Corruption

Another is corrupted when Galatians 1 is read as Paul objecting to a rival denomination rather than denying that a rival gospel exists at all, and when John 14:16 is used to make the Spirit a substitute for Christ rather than a Comforter of the same divine kind.

expand to see more

The pressure on Galatians 1 is always toward pluralism: Paul had his emphasis, the Judaizers had theirs, and the modern reader is invited to regret the heat of the exchange. The grammar refuses this. Paul does not say the other message is a worse gospel or an incomplete gospel; he says it is not another — there is no second item in the category. He then pronounces an anathema twice, which is not the language of a man adjudicating between traditions. Any framework that treats justification by faith alone as one legitimate reading among several has already conceded what Paul spent the letter denying. A gospel that adds a work of the law to the finished work of Christ is not a variant of Christianity. It is its rival.

The corruption at John 14:16 is quieter and more devotional. Another Comforter is often preached as though the Spirit were sent to fill the gap left by an absent Christ — a stand-in for the real thing. But allos means another of the same kind, and the whole point is that nothing is lost in the exchange: the disciples do not trade a divine Person for a lesser influence. This is one of the clearest incidental proofs of the Spirit’s full deity in the Gospels, and treating Him as a substitute quietly demotes the third Person of the Trinity to an instrument. He is not Christ’s replacement; He is Christ’s own promise, of the same rank, given to abide for ever.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two Greek adjectives lie under the single English word, and the New Testament uses the difference deliberately. Where the Authorized Version prints another twice in one sentence, as in Galatians 1:6-7, the reader should assume the Greek has switched words on purpose.

expand to see more

Greek allos (G243) — another of the same kind, one more of the same sort (John 14:16, another Comforter; Galatians 1:7, which is not another).

Greek heteros (G2087) — another of a different kind, a different sort altogether (Galatians 1:6, another gospel; the word behind English heterodox).

Greek euangelion (G2098) — gospel, good news; the noun both adjectives modify in Galatians 1, and the reason the distinction is not academic.

Hebrew achēr — another, other, strange; the word behind the other gods of the first commandment and behind Isaiah 42:8, my glory will I not give to another. Untagged in this lexicon.

Usage

"Another gospel: which is not another (Galatians 1:6-7) — a different kind of message, and therefore not a second gospel at all."

"Another Comforter (John 14:16) is allos: the Spirit is of the same divine kind as the Son, not a lesser stand-in."

"Another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel (2 Corinthians 11:4) — counterfeits travel together, and they travel in threes."
